orchestkit · issue #3215

36 skills nobody could run

A third of the skill library was configured so that neither the user nor the model could invoke it, and nothing reported the fault. Eighteen skills declared 32 dependency edges on those stranded libraries, so the dependency lists silently resolved to nothing.

The obvious fix, un-flagging all 36, turned out to be the wrong one: that flag was also keeping 36 descriptions out of every session's context, and removing it blew the token budget by 1198 tokens per session. So this repairs all 32 edges by un-flagging only the six skills anything actually depends on, and leaves the rest deliberately dormant.

Why it stayed hidden: the errors point at each other

the user types /ork:chain-patterns "can only be invoked by Claude, not directly by users. Ask Claude to use the skill for you."
⇄
so Claude tries Skill(ork:chain-patterns) "cannot be used with Skill tool due to disable-model-invocation"

Each message reads like a routing hint, so it looks recoverable. It is not. Two independent frontmatter flags, user-invocable: false and disable-model-invocation: true, close both doors at once, and nothing warns at authoring time.

The trade the token budget forced

tests/performance/test-token-overhead.sh, on the first attempt

  skill index    ~8025t  (95 model-facing, was 59)
  TOTAL         ~10498t  vs 9300 budget    over by 1198

disable-model-invocation does DOUBLE DUTY. It blocks invocation AND
keeps the description out of every session. Un-flagging all 36 adds
+2638t to every session, forever.

  un-flag all 36          +2638t  -> 10498t   over budget
  un-flag only the 6      + 405t  ->  8969t   fits, 331t spare

The six carry ALL 32 dead edges. The other 30 have no dependants, so
un-flagging them buys zero repaired edges for ~2233t per session.

Their six descriptions were also trimmed by 517 bytes. They were written while the skills were invisible, so nobody paid for the extra words; now that they are model-facing, they have to earn their place in the index.

The 36, by domain

Every one of these was unreachable. The six marked ● freed had dependants, so they were un-flagged and now resolve. The other 30 stay dormant until something actually needs them, at which point the DEAD-EDGE check forces the same fix and the ratchet drops.

The flagship pipeline skills were the worst affected. Every one of them declared libraries it could never load, which is why they behaved thinner than their frontmatter promised.

The fix, two shapes

A. the 6 preload targets: drop the flag, keep the hiding
   chain-patterns · code-review-playbook · architecture-decision-record
   scope-appropriate-architecture · browser-tools · configure
  - disable-model-invocation: true
    user-invocable: false   (kept: still hidden from the slash menu)

B. 6 edges pointed at deliberate user-only actions
   (commit, create-pr, doctor, ci-debug). Those SHOULD stay slash-only,
   so the false dependency was removed instead of weakening them.
  - skills: [commit, review-pr, memory, chain-patterns]
  + skills: [review-pr, memory, chain-patterns]

Never weaken a mutating skill to satisfy a preload. A dependency that cannot resolve is a claim of capability the skill does not have, so the claim is what gets deleted.

The linter that stops it recurring

CheckFails when
UNREACHABLEa skill carries both user-invocable: false and disable-model-invocation: true
DEAD-EDGEa skills: entry names a disable-model-invocation: true target

Not a ratchet. Both counts must be zero, because this sweep took them to zero, so any reappearance is a fresh authoring mistake. Check 1 alone would have caught all 36 on the day each was written. Wired into npm run test:skills; verified to exit 1 against the pre-sweep tree and 0 after.
